title: Give a one-minute brief
summary: Put the main point first and check that the listener knows what to do next.
when: Use this when a classmate or project team needs a quick update with a decision or action.

steps.title: Decide what the listener needs to do
steps.detail: Pick one outcome before you speak. For example, ask your group to confirm who will bring the printed handouts.

steps.title: Open with the request
steps.detail: Say what you need in the first sentence. Try “Please confirm who will bring the handouts to tomorrow’s practice.”

steps.title: Give just enough context
steps.detail: Add the facts the listener needs to act, such as the number of copies and when they’re needed. Use familiar words and explain any acronym that matters.

steps.title: Choose a channel that fits
steps.detail: Use a quick message for a simple update. If people need to discuss the decision, speak live and leave time for questions.

steps.title: Ask for a reply you can check
steps.detail: Ask who will do it and by when. Listen to the answer, correct any mismatch, and confirm the agreed action.

check: The listener can repeat the action, who owns it, and when it’s due.
avoid: Treating silence as confirmation or burying the request under background.

title: Coach one behavior at a time
summary: Turn an observation into a small change the other person can practice.
when: Use this after a classroom brief, rehearsal, or routine team task, while both people can still recall what happened.

steps.title: Name the moment
steps.detail: Choose one specific point in the task. Try “When we switched to the last slide in today’s rehearsal…”

steps.title: Describe what you saw
steps.detail: Say what happened in terms the other person could verify. For example, “The due date was on the slide but didn’t come up in the explanation.”

steps.title: Ask how it went for them
steps.detail: Invite their account first. Listen for context you missed and explain the effect you observed, such as two people leaving with different dates.

steps.title: Agree on a small adjustment
steps.detail: Ask what they would do next time. Set a practice goal tied to the issue, such as saying the date aloud before opening questions.

steps.title: Look for the adjustment next time
steps.detail: Check that behavior at the next rehearsal. Acknowledge when they make the change and close the loop.

check: Both people can name the behavior to practice and how they’ll tell whether it improved.
avoid: Stacking several criticisms together or guessing why someone acted a certain way.

title: Plan backward from a deadline
summary: Turn one fixed deadline into a short timeline the group can actually follow.
when: Use this classroom exercise when your team has a fixed presentation time and several tasks to finish first.

steps.title: Start with the finish time
steps.detail: Write the deadline and what counts as ready. For a 3 p.m. presentation, the deck is open, roles are clear, and the group can start on time.

steps.title: Put the last check just before it
steps.detail: Decide when the group needs to rehearse or open the deck together. Leave time to make corrections before the presentation.

steps.title: Work back through dependencies
steps.detail: Place tasks in reverse order. The rehearsal needs a merged deck, and the merged deck needs everyone’s slides.

steps.title: Protect the team’s preparation time
steps.detail: Try the lesson’s one-third/two-thirds split as a classroom rule of thumb. For a 90-minute window, aim to give the group its direction in about 30 minutes so it has about 60 to prepare.

steps.title: Check and share the timeline
steps.detail: Give each milestone one owner. Compare the times in the schedule and on the slides before sharing a single version.

check: Every milestone has a time and owner, and the group can point to the time reserved for rehearsal or corrections.
avoid: Using most of the available time to perfect the plan before the group can start.

title: Reconcile a training inventory
summary: Compare an authorized equipment count with the record and flag any difference for follow-up.
when: Use this for a classroom kit or demo equipment you’re authorized to count. Follow the custodian’s inventory process.

steps.title: Agree on what is being counted
steps.detail: Ask the custodian which items and approved record are in scope. For a practice run, use mock entries for a classroom kit.

steps.title: Count what you can verify
steps.detail: Work through the list with the responsible person. For each line, compare the recorded count with what you can physically verify.

steps.title: Record the difference plainly
steps.detail: Keep the expected and observed counts separate. For example, record “6 listed, 5 counted, 1 unresolved” so the gap stays visible.

steps.title: Flag the discrepancy
steps.detail: Bring the difference and any supporting records to the custodian. Distinguish what you verified from explanations that still need checking.

steps.title: Follow the authorized update process
steps.detail: Keep the item open until the custodian resolves it and updates the record through the proper process. Confirm the count and the final disposition agree.

check: Someone reviewing the inventory can tell what was counted, what is unresolved, and who is following up.
avoid: Changing the record to make the count match before the discrepancy is resolved.

title: Check before sharing a file
summary: Work through a short sharing decision using a fictional classroom document.
when: Use this classroom exercise to practice the checks that come before sending information. Work with a mock document and fictional recipients.

steps.title: Read the document’s markings
steps.detail: Start with the handling information provided in the exercise. If it is unclear, mark the decision as pending and ask the document owner what rules apply.

steps.title: Check who actually needs it
steps.detail: List the intended recipients and the work each needs the file for. Check the authorization required by the exercise for each recipient.

steps.title: Confirm permission and channel
steps.detail: Identify who can authorize the transfer and which channel the exercise permits for that information. Wait for clarification if either is missing.

steps.title: Record the decision
steps.detail: Use the practice log to capture what would be shared, with whom, under whose authorization, and through which channel.

steps.title: Practice the escalation
steps.detail: If the scenario says the file went to the wrong recipient, identify the designated reporting contact and flag the suspected disclosure promptly.

check: You can point to the recipient’s need, the authorization, the approved channel, and the reporting contact.
avoid: Assuming that a familiar recipient or a convenient chat channel is enough to authorize a transfer.

title: Write one cyber risk entry
summary: Connect an asset, a threat, and a weakness to a concrete effect and next action.
when: Use this classroom exercise for a fictional group workspace, such as a shared copy of the presentation slides.

steps.title: Choose one asset
steps.detail: Name the file, service, or device and what the group relies on it for. For example, the group needs its shared slide deck to present on Friday.

steps.title: Describe what could go wrong
steps.detail: Write a threat and the weakness that makes it possible. Accidental edits are the threat. Broad edit permissions are the weakness.

steps.title: Describe the effect
steps.detail: Say what changes if it happens. Slides may become inaccurate, which affects integrity, or the group may lose access to a usable deck, which affects availability.

steps.title: Judge likelihood and impact
steps.detail: Explain how plausible it is given the scenario and how much it would disrupt the group. Mark missing evidence as an assumption.

steps.title: Pick an action and a check
steps.detail: Suggest one step that addresses the weakness, such as giving most participants view access, and say how the authorized owner could verify the result.

check: Your entry reads as one clear chain from asset and weakness to impact, with an action that reduces the risk.
avoid: Listing a weakness without explaining its effect or assigning a precise score without supporting evidence.

title: Read a modeled radio link
summary: Separate terrain clearance, predicted received level, and margin when reading a saved result.
when: Use this for a classroom interpretation exercise with a saved model or a fictional path between points A and B.

steps.title: Identify the model inputs
steps.detail: Write down the band, transmitter power, antenna heights, gains, and losses shown for the run. Keep these alongside the result so it’s clear which settings produced it.

steps.title: Read the path profile
steps.detail: Check the legend and distinguish a clear optical path from terrain in the path. Notice whether the model also reports clearance around the direct path, called Fresnel clearance.

steps.title: Read the level and margin separately
steps.detail: Received level is shown in dBm. Subtract the model’s receiver threshold from the predicted received level to find the margin in dB. In a fictional run, −90 dBm against −100 dBm gives 10 dB of margin.

steps.title: Explain the result in a sentence
steps.detail: Say whether terrain blocks the direct path and whether the model still predicts a usable signal. The worked example shows both outcomes can occur together.

steps.title: Mark it as a prediction
steps.detail: Keep the model result and any authorized real-world check in separate fields. For this exercise, leave the field result blank if all you have is a screenshot.

check: You can explain the predicted margin and terrain clearance separately and name the inputs used.
avoid: Reading a modeled pass as measured coverage or comparing results without checking their settings.

title: Compare current and target safeguards
summary: Use a small NIST profile to turn a gap into an action your group can track.
when: Use this classroom exercise to compare what a fictional team does today with what it wants to achieve.

steps.title: Set the boundary
steps.detail: Pick one workflow, such as how your class group accounts for shared presentation files. Write down what is in scope and any assumptions you made.

steps.title: Gather the information you have
steps.detail: List the mock rules, practices, roles, and tools in the scenario. Use those details when describing the current state.

steps.title: Pair current with target
steps.detail: Pick one outcome from the framework. For example, for data inventory, write “The group knows the slide deck exists” under current and “The group keeps a list of designated shared files” under target.

steps.title: Write down the gap
steps.detail: Explain what has to change and which part matters most. Turn that difference into one action with an owner and a date to review it.

steps.title: Recheck after the change
steps.detail: Review the action against the target. Update the current description only when you have evidence that the change happened.

check: Each target has a corresponding current entry and a visible next action if there’s a gap.
avoid: Treating an intended safeguard as already in place.

sources.title: Steps for creating and using a profile

title: Review a file access request
summary: Practice separating who is asking, what they need, and what the policy permits.
when: Use this paper exercise with a fictional class folder. Give a classmate a mock request to view a handout from a device described in the scenario.

steps.title: Name the request
steps.detail: Write the requester, the device, the file, and the action. A request to view one handout is specific enough to assess.

steps.title: Check identity and device separately
steps.detail: Read the mock policy and identify what it requires you to know about the requester and the device. Mark any missing evidence as unknown.

steps.title: Check authorization for that file
steps.detail: Decide whether the requester’s role and reason meet the policy for the file. A verified identity answers who is asking. The policy answers whether they may access it.

steps.title: Choose the smallest permission
steps.detail: If the mock policy permits access, choose the minimum permission needed for that request. For viewing a handout, that means read access to the handout.

steps.title: Test a changed request
steps.detail: Change one detail, such as a request to edit the file or a different device. Apply the policy again and explain whether the decision changes.

check: You can explain the decision using the identity, device, resource, and permission required for this request.
avoid: Using access to one file or presence on a trusted network as permission for every request.

sources.title: Verify explicitly and grant least privilege

title: Work through an ethical decision
summary: Compare feasible choices when speed, accuracy, and responsibility pull in different directions.
when: Use this classroom exercise when a fictional group discovers a mistake in the attendance totals just before submitting a report.

steps.title: Name the tension
steps.detail: Write down the competing duties. The group wants to meet the deadline, and the person using the report needs an accurate total.

steps.title: Find the rules and duties
steps.detail: Use the mock submission instructions to find who approves the report and what to do if a total is still being checked. Note any requirement you need to confirm.

steps.title: List feasible choices
steps.detail: Compare options such as recounting before submission, filing a clearly marked provisional total if the procedure allows it, or asking the reviewer how to handle the deadline.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.detail: Ask whether each option follows the rules, what happens to the people relying on the record, and what a responsible leader would be willing to stand behind.

steps.title: Decide and reflect
steps.detail: Pick the option you can justify, say who needs to know, and explain what you’d do differently to prevent the same problem next time.

check: You can explain the choice using a rule, a likely consequence, and a duty or value.
avoid: Choosing the fastest action before checking whose work depends on the record.

title: Study leadership through a short scene
summary: Turn a film clip or classroom role-play into evidence you can discuss.
when: Use this classroom exercise after a short scene that shows someone guiding a team through a problem.

steps.title: Pick one moment
steps.detail: Choose a short exchange with a clear decision or interaction. Write one line about what the group needed at that point.

steps.title: Record the action
steps.detail: Note the timestamp or scene cue and describe what the person said or did. For example, “She asked each group to explain its blocker before assigning a task.”

steps.title: Connect it to a competency
steps.detail: Use the lesson’s leading, developing, and achieving categories. Explain which fits the action and how you can tell from the scene.

steps.title: Trace the effect
steps.detail: Record what happened next, such as a teammate taking ownership or a timeline becoming clear. If the clip ends first, mark the effect as unknown.

steps.title: Share one observation
steps.detail: Give a partner the scene cue, action, category, and evidence. Ask them which detail best supports the category you chose.

check: Your partner can find the same moment and understand why you chose that competency.
avoid: Giving a general impression of the character without pointing to a specific action.

title: Study with a worked example
summary: Try a classroom task first, then use the sample to see how the reasoning works.
when: Use this method with an assigned classroom exercise that has a worked solution. Start with one part of the exercise if time is short.

steps.title: Pick a specific part to practice
steps.detail: Choose a small output you can finish, such as the timeline or the format of a presentation. Read the requirement before opening the worked solution.

steps.title: Draft your answer first
steps.detail: Write your own attempt and mark assumptions or places where you had to make a choice. Keep the draft so you can see what changed.

steps.title: Compare the reasoning
steps.detail: Find the matching part of the sample. Read the notes explaining why the example works and look for the requirement each choice serves.

steps.title: Separate mistakes from valid differences
steps.detail: Mark any mismatch with the stated requirement. If your answer differs from the sample but still meets the requirement, write one sentence defending your choice.

steps.title: Revise and explain
steps.detail: Change the weakest part, then explain the revision aloud without reading from the sample. Use the handout reference beside the example if the reason remains unclear.

check: You can identify one change you made and the requirement or evidence behind it.
avoid: Reading the sample first and treating its wording as the only correct answer.

sources.title: How to use the worked sample
